rationale: A control panel at a power plant, with a prosthetic human wired in as operator; it points at automated plant operation but says nothing of a self-running, self-maintaining plant of robots.
Locks released by a combination of thought waves match the idea of controlling a device by thought. No mechanism is given, and the 1998 case was a cursor moved by an implanted patient.
Trucks guided by a robot-control system that may go out of whack hints at automated road vehicles, but the quote only warns of a malfunction and says nothing of a vehicle driving itself with cameras.
A servoconsole dialed to show a breakfast menu on a viewscreen is a home service console, but the quote gives no automatic response to occupants as in a self-run house.
A cyborg uses his own brain as the calculator for orbit and objective; the function of computing orbits matches but a human mind, not an onboard machine, does it.
Data put to calculating machines to check predictions is generic computation; it lacks the code-breaking use and any programmability or electronic detail of Colossus.
A mechanical doll made as the ideal undemanding woman points toward a companion robot, but a robot pet sold as a consumer product is a different kind of companionship.
Records on a central computer's tubes are deleted by voice order; this concerns erasing stored records, not finding items matching a query, so only loosely related to search.
A machine registrar that converses with personality and answers questions from data matches question answering in function; how it works is not given and the quote shows only its petulant tone.
A chrome robot escort that comes gliding out for a boy is a personal robot companion, but nothing in the quote about it provides affection or play like a robot pet.
Computers narrowing the error circle on where wreckage will fall is orbit prediction, which matches the function of computing orbits; it is ground tracking, not onboard maneuvering.
A single Master Machine whose destruction halts all robots worldwide matches a central computer directing robots; a warehouse system coordinating mobile robots is far narrower in scope.

Each person inserts a key into a reader that makes contact with an electronic device to gain entry to the hangar: key-based machine-checked access, though the key is a physical key rather than an encoded card.

A cabinet that projects a captive's thoughts as 3D moving pictures is a volumetric display only in loose terms; the picture source is a brain recorder, and the hologram milestone is about display technology.
Machines controlled by electronic analogues of brains in a factory points at automated production, but the quote says nothing of a plant running unsupervised or robots building robots.
A machine that hears questions and answers from a huge microtape store matches answering questions in function; the quote leaves out how it understands language.
A chart projection screen showing the fleet's position in space matches a live position display; the quote lacks radar tracks or computer processing of sensor input.
A deaf man producing eloquent text with a composition machine is manual operation of a writing contraption, not data-to-text generation; the quote is satire and shows no automatic composing.
Copying a person's brain pattern into a positronic robot to make a replica is an android double of a person, but the Lincoln figure is a scripted animatronic, not a copied mind.
A giant computer with sensory organs near mind-reading and lie-detecting is vague; no brain signals are read and no specific thoughts or images are extracted.
The quote is a remark about philosophy and abstract thought and says nothing of a machine producing text; the claim about a story formula is not in the passage.
The belief that machines answer everyday problems and a superior one can predict the future is only a general claim about answering machines, with no mechanism or language use.
Pressing buttons on a console makes a machine produce a packet of cards from a person's record: retrieval of stored records on request, with no mention of a search query over a large collection.
A servo-tracer that goes to sleep in police use suggests a machine for tracking a target, but the quote gives no detail of how or whether a person is located or reported.
Robots designed as traffic police that also drive cars and think point at robotic driving in general terms; no vehicle sensing or route-following mechanism is described.
A local machine refers hard questions to a master System Computer on Luna; it hints at a networked answering computer but the quote has no knowledge base or language handling.
A computer that takes English logic puzzles without humans translating into binary matches understanding questions in natural language; ELIZA only matched patterns in typed text.
Waiters are humanoid robots remote-controlled by a central robot brain, which matches one computer directing a population of robots; the restaurant context differs from warehouse fulfilment.
Control over machines via electronic detection of thought waves matches thought-controlled devices; no sensing method or user is described, and the real case used an implant.
Stripping a person's mind layer by layer to extract hidden information is mind extraction in loose terms; there is no device description or images, and the real case reconstructed viewed images.
Saying the best pattern for the machine would be the human brain nods at brain-modeled computing but gives no interconnected units or learning, so it does not describe a working network.
A little machine that takes orders from the control room and adjusts every machine below matches central control of automated machinery; no unattended or self-maintaining plant is described.
A shipboard computer that analyses incident data and prints answers on facsimile tape is a machine that answers questions, though the quote shows only the output mechanism, not language input.
Human directors operate a fleet of robots over many ships and aircraft; the quote points to remote coordination but by people, not by a central computer.

The ship's computer computes orbits, speeds and distances for pinpointing a spot in the Asteroid Belt, matching the orbit calculation function; the interplanetary context differs from the 1965 near-Earth flight.
Robots controlled telepathically through a helmet match controlling machines by thought; the mechanism is only a helmet transmitter and the real case was a cursor.
Patrol cars read magnetic tags and send the data to a central records computer for instant checks: machine-read identification feeding a database, though for vehicle checks, not granting access.
An electrode clamped to a witness's head lets a device print a sketch of a remembered face, which matches reading images from a brain; the 2008 case reconstructed viewed images, not remembered ones.
A huge 3D tank with millions of lights tracking fleet units matches a live positions display; the volumetric form goes beyond the console of radar tracks in SAGE.

Electrodes pick up subvocal nerve impulses and a computer turns them into words: this is signal-to-speech, but the milestone concerns a talking calculator and reading machine producing voice from text.
A mechanical musicometer that composes sonatas by mathematical rule and a handle matches machine composition of music; CSIRAC only played music and was a digital computer.
Android duplicates of workers built from a photograph take over assignments, a copy of specific individuals, but the Lincoln animatronic is a scripted figure of one man, not worker replacement.
A button press quickly flips a person's card into a slot: instant retrieval of a personal record, but mechanical and without search over a large collection.
A city-wide library serving remote requests for recorded images and records on demand matches remote retrieval of stored items; no matching query by machine is stated.
The quotation is about something left unfinished after a jump and says nothing about a database or retrieval; the summary's library is not in the quote.
Cubes piloting aircars are ruled by telepathy and will, matching thought control of machines; no sensing or implant mechanism is given.
Computers fed live data compute the likelihood of future events and predict where an assassin will appear, which matches predictive policing; the real milestone was a database of wanted persons.
An android self that laughs as the human duplicate does presumes an exact double of a specific person, but the quote shows no mechanism and a stage animatronic is a much weaker double.
Circuits made by electroplating and growing crystals instead of wiring each connection matches the idea of integrated, solid-state circuits; the process is only sketched.
Energy beings that would beat any calculator at answering any question point to omniscient answering, but they are not a computer and no language interface is described.
An executive speaks a demand into a mouthpiece and gets a printed summary within moments: voice input to a machine that responds, but the Apricot's commands were for a computer, not statistics.
A helmet used to scan a person's mind and psychology is evocative of brain reading, but it states no readout of specific thoughts or images.
Roboticians, supervisors and a foreman point to a place run with few people, but the quote only lists staff and says nothing of the work being automated.
An implant that scans nearby nervous systems and relays physiological data and subvocal speech to its host is an electronic body device, but not one restoring a sense like the cochlear implant.
A replacement document is obtained within seconds from a filing computer, matching fast retrieval of stored records; no query matching is described.
A portable projector inflating a transparent globe that displays solar-system models is a volumetric picture, but nothing is said of a hologram or its imaging method.
A character looks up a planet in the Galactic Directory aboard ship: lookup in a large stored collection, matching retrieval in function, but the mechanism is unstated.
A robo-pilot and astrogational computers installed in a spaceship match onboard guidance and course computing; the quote gives no orbital burns or any detail.
An automatic translating secretary that reviews a diplomatic agreement is a machine secretary summarizing, loosely akin to dictation, with no sign it converts speech to text.
Punched buttons on a reference panel bring screening cards from the information bank, matching retrieval of stored data by code; a panel lookup is simpler than a query system.
A videophone linked to a records database that shows a personal brief on screen matches online retrieval of records; the display and phone context goes beyond the 1966 system.
An ambulance with a computer circuit that conveys limited ideas relays a thought translator; the quote's own machine is a vehicle circuit, not a decoder of speech.
Directions computed by a mechanical brain and fed into an autopilot for lunar landing match computing a course and steering a craft; the milestone is orbital maneuvers in Earth orbit.
A supercomputer holding all human knowledge and predicting events is an oracle; the quote gives no question answering in language and goes well beyond what START did.
Automatic integrating course plotters keep a vessel on its calculated course, matching onboard course computing; the quote is a display of instruments with no burns calculated.
A computer does in thirty seconds a navigation calculation that would take a human fifty thousand years: course computation by machine, though for hyperspace navigation.
Street information robots answer questions from memory banks, matching a machine answering questions publicly; the quote gives no language handling.
A helmet relays what a mind learns in an alien body to a ship's electronic brain; a link from brain to machine but it is a transfer of experience, not a device control.
Schooling direct from the Brain, tapping its informational resources, is about a central knowledge source for teaching, not coordination of robots.
A stone worn on a finger opens and activates the vehicle: a token that grants access, similar to a machine-read token, but the stone is not an encoded card.
Feeding every shred of information to the Brain so it names the right person is an answering oracle, but the quote has no questions asked in ordinary language.
A cybernetic robot with a memory bank serving as a ship system and subject to electronic fatigue; the quote gives no sign it calculates orbits or steers.
Robots powered and directed by a short-wave transmitter match remote operation; the operator seeing or feeling through the robot is not in the quote.
A pointing device picks out a light on a display and the number flashes up, a live display with identification of tracked fleets; the milestone is radar track consoles with light pens.
An elecalc computes interstellar flight courses, matching course computation, though the quote itself is about asking it to make a bet.
A wristband starts a helicopter, a worn token granting machine access; it matches in function but a wristband is not a card read by a reader.
A single programming head actuating eight assemblies delivering modules in a continuous stream matches automated production; it lacks lights-out operation or robots maintaining themselves.
A machine that reads your mind and retranslates it into visual images for you to watch matches reconstructing images from brain signals; the ATR work was crude 10x10 pixels.
Pressing button combinations on a console while a typer prints out data matches a retrieval console; the quote does not say the system found matches in a large collection.
A registrar machine that talks with feminine petulance matches a machine conversing in ordinary language; ELIZA relied on pattern matching with far less personality.
An audioscriber transcribes a conversational exchange for the secretary, matching a machine turning speech into text, with no mention of how it works.
A master wristband opens any apartment door, a token granting access to locked doors, matching access tokens in function but not an encoded card.
Punching the ship's computer to compute landing trajectories matches an onboard computer; the quote offers no maneuver detail.
A whistled code word opens the door automatically: a device obeys a sound command, matching voice-command in function; whistling is not recognition of words.
Robots with radioatomic brains react to telepathic commands sent through helmet transmitters; a person controls remote robots, but by thought and with no senses relayed back.
A keyboard feeds a remote orrery computer that returns an asteroid's exact position in seconds, matching orbit computation, but it is a ground tool rather than shipboard.
A fleet coordination division using semantic calculators is only a hint of computing for command; the quote includes no analysis of battle data or planning.
A calculator gives course results and gyroscopes lock the ship onto a new trajectory, matching calculating a course and steering along it; the real flight was a crewed orbital maneuver.
A machine with a million times the human synapses and molecular memory is a giant brain; the quote shows no interconnected neurons that learn, or any use.
The quotation is a threat shouting at a person and describes no machine; the calculator in the summary is not there.
Screens that capture the deeps of the subconscious and turn them into pictures match showing mental images on a screen; the mechanism is not given and the 2020 case decoded speech into text.
Attaching motor and sensory buds to nerves in a machine brain is wiring nerve-like units, but it is physical hand-building, not a trained network recognizing digits.
A computer that has solved all crimes by correlating factors matches computer crime solving in function, though the 1967 NCIC was a database of wanted persons rather than an inference engine.
Machines are said to outdo playwrights and novelists for creativity, but this is a claim without any mechanism or description of how a computer composes text.
A master robot supplies power and commands to a team of lesser robots, matching one machine directing many; the milestone is a warehouse deployment of mobile robots.
Running all the robberies for a period through the police computer to find unsolved matches is computer analysis of crime records; NCIC was lookup of wanted persons, narrower.
A small shipboard computer works out orbital and positional data in flight, matching onboard orbit calculation; blast intensity is part of the burn planning as well.
Questions are submitted to a council machine brain on microtapes and answers are broadcast: a machine answering questions, but no natural language is involved.
An electromechanical Educator so valuable a man would murder for it is a teaching machine in name only; the quote says nothing about lessons or grading.
A planet-sized maintenance, propulsion and manufacturing complex that runs largely by itself matches a self-running plant, but with few details on how.
The man's expression changes after something verifies him; the quote is a reaction scene and does not say what is scanned, so it does not support retina scanning.
The claim that the Machine never makes mistakes about matching people points to a pairing computer, but the quote is just an assertion and says nothing about traits compared.
Visi-chambers where people spend most of their lives dreaming match immersive entertainment in function; the mechanism of feeding senses is not given.
Robots that are telepaths and learned to think from humans is a claim about reading minds, but it is stated by robots with no machine reading brain signals.
A super-robot with its creator's qualities magnified is a robot modelled on a person, but it is not an exact double and the quote has no sign of copying.

Instead of printed figures you see the war with complete visual and auditory hallucinations: a computer-generated world fed to the senses, which matches VR, with brain stimulation rather than goggles.
A national security logic computer asked about its own security hints at a machine consulted for answers, but the quote has no language interface.
The quote says telepathic communication with a machine is considered far in the future, which is a remark of expectation and not a described device.
A combat computer computes odds each instant and retreats when losing, matching a machine that calculates battle outcomes; the SAGE computers handled air defence tracking.
A doll made in a woman's image as an ideal woman is a replica of a particular person in function, but the Lincoln animatronic is a scripted figure of a historical man.
Cameras record intruders and the pictures are matched to ident-card records at police HQ: identification from images matched to records, though the matching is not described.
General-purpose robots controlled by radio signals and orders as colony workers match remote operation of robots; the manipulator milestone gives the operator sight and feel.
A giant robot's brain picks up the operator's mental directions, matching device control by thought; the interface is unexplained and cannot be built with 1998 tech.
Automaton men purchasable and rejected by the speaker as pretty: companion robots in function, but with no sign of affection or any mechanism.
A machine intelligence that reads minds and makes illusions tailored to thoughts is vague, with no readout of specific images.
An atomic-pile powered factory that combines materials with worn-out robots to keep producing indefinitely matches a self-running plant of robots building robots; the Fanuc plant lasted a few weeks.
A screen records the thought-wave impulses of an audience and synthesizes them into a display: brain signals turned into images, though with an audience composite instead of a person's image.
A polite robot voice at the door asks the visitor's name, a machine speaking with an artificial voice; the milestone is a talking calculator and a reading machine.
A freed mind quickly calculates the time for the first braking burn; the function of computing a burn matches but a mind and not a computer does it.
A bag opens when a photocell recognizes the owner's thumbprint, matching automatic fingerprint authentication; the real 1965 work was automated analysis for identification.

The ship measures gravitation, acceleration and angular velocity, computes course data and finds its way: inertial guidance by an onboard computer, close to the function; the real flight was in orbit.
A scripto that types spoken words onto paper matches dictation transcription in function; the quote only says it needed a transformer, with no detail.
Radio waves read the electrical synapse patterns of thought, like a mine detector reading metal: remote brain reading in principle, but with no readout of content.
The quotation is a philosophical claim about uniting mind and matter and says nothing about a machine reading thoughts or images.
A vocowriter used with a special voice matches a voice-driven writing machine; the need for a special voice resembles early discrete dictation.
The ship's calculator identifies a star from spectrograph data and prints SOL, which matches navigation computing by identifying position; it is not a burn calculator.
The ship's computer shows the ship's position on a 3D galactic chart, matching navigational position computing; the quote itself says only that the ship's position is being discussed.
An indexograph reports a man's character and shows an ideograph of thoughts: a machine reading mind and display in function, though the passage only reports a character reading.
Robots overloaded by contradictory orders from their supervisor shows a robot supervisor giving commands; there is no central computer coordinating many robots.
A central robot computer is reprogrammed with a new repair problem so that robots dismantle a man: one computer directing many robots, shown through misuse.
Robotic horses steered by the rider's thoughts match controlling machines by thought; the interface is not explained, and the implants of 1998 gave only cursor control.
A hidden device checks the whorls of a militiaman's fingerprints and opens a door: automatic fingerprint recognition used for access, matching the function of authentication.
Police robots' telelenses report everything to the Brain beneath the city, a central computer directing a population of robots; a warehouse system is narrower.
Agents drive cars with detectors until they pick up a person's thought pattern: tracking a person by an emitted signal, but not a worn tag reporting position.
An automatic computer figures the distance, velocity and time needed for a landing: onboard computation of a maneuver, close to the function.
A machine-reporter of thoughts and feelings is named only; the quote gives no mechanism, and no text results.
A glowing three-dimensional image of the Solar System before the viewer matches a volumetric display; the quote does not say how it is made.
An apparatus on the head collects thought vibrations as you think and reproduces them: a head device reading thoughts, matching function but vague on the mechanism.
A dicto-typer is a machine that transcribes dictation to typed text, matching in function; nothing in the quote says how.
Participants in a simulation obey rules and a simulated death; the quote shows a computer-generated world convincing enough to feel real, but only the rules are cited.
Each thought vibration is converted into a unique light quality, a display of thought as light, but not text or images.

Machines that originate problems and make other machines is about machine intelligence designing machines, and loosely suggests computers designing computers, but nothing about using a computer to design parts.
A computer judge hears facts and issues a ruling by synthesized voice, so a machine speaks in an artificial voice; the quote itself only shows the casing.
A screen that rises from a dining table and shows a bill of fare when the diner sits is a display of information in place of paper; CRT displays on Whirlwind served a radar purpose.
The linotype sets a verse not in the copy, writing by itself; it is a machine creating text but with no data, mechanism or generation described.
A computer assembles recorded words to answer a child's endless questions, matching answering questions in natural language; it differs from the text-based internet system.
Appliances tune themselves to their owners' habits and work right, matching a house adapting to its occupants; ECHO IV was a household controller.
A calculating machine selects mates to produce superior offspring, matching a computer pairing people; the basis is genetic traits rather than questionnaire answers.
Autopilot computers with preset tapes handle astrogation and the jump sequence, matching onboard computing and steering of a craft; the quote itself is a pilot checking clocks.
A plastic ID disk dropped into a slot makes a voder announce the holder: a machine reads an identity token and speaks with an artificial voice; the voder predates 1948.
